final:
In May of 1979, a Chicago commodities broker walked out his front door, told his family he'd be back after a business meeting, and never came back. Years passed, a court declared him legally dead, and his wife and three children began collecting survivor benefits from the Social Security Administration.

Joanne Jones would later recall the specific thing her husband said before he sped away from their suburban Chicago home: "The meeting is not in a business office." That was the whole explanation.

He was 40 years old, and he left dressed wrong for a business meeting — tennis shirt and slacks instead of the corporate attire his wife knew. Small detail. The kind of thing a person files away and only retrieves later, when they're trying to reconstruct the last ordinary morning. What she couldn't have filed away in the moment was the bracelet, left behind when he rushed out the door. He was frazzled enough leaving that he forgot to put it on.

By May 11, Joanne had reported him missing. Investigators eventually found his silver Buick and a pair of sunglasses near O'Hare International Airport. The car near the airport suggested travel.

He had not always been the kind of man who needed to run. Jones had come up through the unglamorous end of Chicago commerce — delivery boy for his future father-in-law's liquor store, a place called Mr. Joseph's Liquor Cabinet, where he eventually worked his way up to manager. He married the owner's daughter. From that starting point, he had climbed to the floor of the Chicago Board of Trade, trading commodities in one of the most competitive financial arenas in the country. The ranch home in the suburbs came with a volleyball court. By any visible measure, the life was a success.

But the gambling had left him with giant debts. His wife later told authorities he once lost $30,000 on a single basketball game — not a slow bleed, one bet. When the debts outpaced what trading could cover, he forged Joanne's name on a second mortgage application to keep cash moving. And then, a few months before he walked out that door, he sold his seat on the Board of Trade entirely — his professional identity, his income, his standing — to cover $210,000 in accumulated debt. His wife said he kept going into Chicago to work afterward, though it was unclear for whom, and she suspected it was for the mob.

What happened next made the calculus of staying untenable. In April 1979, a fellow commodities trader was shot and killed in his suburban home by masked intruders. Court papers would later say Jones left shortly after that shooting specifically to get a fresh start. The walls of the life he had built were coming down in a specific order.

Before he could become someone else, he needed paper. That was the whole problem — not distance, not disguise, not a new city. A man without documents is still the man he was. By his own account to authorities, Jones paid an associate $800 for three things: a fake Illinois driver's license, a fake birth certificate, and a Social Security number that belonged to a real, living person. The name attached to all of it was Joseph Richard Sandelli.

What $800 bought in 1979 was not a disguise. It was a legal existence. A driver's license says you are who you say you are. A birth certificate says you were born as who you say you are. A Social Security number says the government has been tracking you your whole life as who you say you are. Stack all three and you have something closer to a person than most forgeries ever manage — a coherent paper trail with a beginning, a middle, and a present. Arthur Jones didn't need to erase himself. He needed to overwrite himself, and the three documents together did exactly that.

The Social Security number came from a man named Clifton Goodenough. Jones, by his own account to authorities, admitted buying Goodenough's number specifically, not a randomly generated fake, but a real number attached to a real man. A stolen number, belonging to a real person, passes the check that a fabricated one does not.

From Chicago, Jones didn't go straight to Las Vegas. After disappearing, he skipped around the country, stopping in California and Florida before eventually settling in Las Vegas. Each stop put more geography between Arthur Gerald Jones and the life that had collapsed behind him. The criminal complaint would later describe it plainly: he was "fleeing the mob" and "starting a new life." Both things were true at once. Joseph Richard Sandelli was the instrument that made the second one possible.

Seven years after Jones walked out that door, an Illinois court did what the law does when a person stays gone long enough: it declared Arthur Gerald Jones legally dead. The year was 1986. His wife and three children had been living without him, and the court's ruling converted that absence into a formal legal status — not missing, not disappeared, but dead. And death, on paper, triggers a payment.

That money was real. The death that justified it was not. Jones was alive in 1986 while a court certified his nonexistence and the federal government cut checks to the people he had abandoned.

He didn't just escape consequences. His disappearance, once certified by a court, generated $47,000 in Social Security survivor benefits for his family. The question the rest of this story has to answer is who, exactly, was left holding the bill.

Las Vegas absorbed Joseph Richard Sandelli the way it absorbs most people who need to stop being someone else — without asking questions. By the 1980s, Jones had settled into the city and found work that matched the one skill his old life had genuinely sharpened: reading odds. According to his attorney, he went to work at the Desert Inn first, then moved into sports book operations at a local casino. At the time investigators caught up with him, he was working the sport and race book at the Rampart. The career he landed in was not entirely foreign to the one he had left behind, both turned on numbers, risk, and the movement of money.

He and his longtime girlfriend lived on a block of stucco homes, dusty lots, and a few horse corrals. Their neighbors registered almost nothing about them. Leslie Lamoya, who lives down the street, told reporters she had been there ten years and never once seen the man. Another neighbor had only a single image to offer: Jones and his girlfriend bringing in the newspaper, watering plants. That was the whole of it. No friction, no memorable moment, no face that stuck.

His attorney, Stephen Stein, explained the girlfriend's position plainly: she and her family knew him only as Joseph Richard Sandelli. "They had no idea about anything," Stein said, "which makes sense. Common sense tells you the guy's not going to go around telling anybody about this kind of thing."

His girlfriend and her family knew him only as Sandelli, and that held for decades. Arthur Gerald Jones, as a daily operational matter, had ceased to exist.

Clifton Goodenough had never worked at a Las Vegas casino. He was a nurse at a Phoenix veterans hospital, and the closest he got to the sports book industry was a longtime feud with the IRS over income he supposedly had earned in Las Vegas. The IRS kept coming after him over that "extra income" every year since 1995. He pushed back. The IRS pushed harder. Before it was over, the agency had garnished his wages and pulled money directly from his bank account. His family absorbed that disruption year after year, fighting a paper record that insisted he was someone he was not.

When he reported to the Social Security Administration that his statements showed income from Las Vegas casinos where he had never worked, the investigation led to the Nevada Department of Motor Vehicles, which had issued a driver's license in 1988 to Joseph Richard Sandelli using Goodenough's Social Security number. The license had been renewed since. In May 2008, he renewed it at a Henderson DMV office. Jones walked in as Sandelli, handed over the number that belonged to a nurse in Phoenix, and walked out with a fresh license.

That renewal is what investigators found when they pulled the DMV file. They contacted the DMV, and had their thread. In July 2011, state and federal investigators arrested him in Las Vegas, and when they asked whether he was the Chicago trader who had vanished 32 years earlier, he said yes.

One more renewal, and it might have lasted longer. In the end, an Arizona nurse's tax fight reached the right desk, and Joseph Richard Sandelli stopped existing.

Arthur Gerald Jones stood before Clark County District Judge James Bixler on January 31, 2012, as himself — his real name, his real record, his real age. He was 73 years old.

The plea he had entered the previous September covered one felony count: using a false name to obtain a driver's license or identity card. That single count was the product of a deal with prosecutors that let him avoid trial on several additional felony charges, including identity theft. One count, one guilty plea, and the rest folded away into the agreement. What remained was the sentencing, and Judge Bixler had a specific question before imposing it. He asked Jones directly how he intended to pay back the money.

The answer came from Jones's attorney, Stephen Stein: the restitution would come out of his Social Security benefits.

The mechanism the court chose was precise. The court ordered Jones to repay the Social Security Administration for the survivor benefits his family had collected after he was declared legally dead. His own Social Security benefits, his attorney said, would be the source of repayment for what his fictional death had extracted from the government decades earlier.

Beyond what he owed the Social Security Administration, Judge Bixler also ordered Jones to pay about $11,400 to Clifton Goodenough, compensation for the missed work and legal fees Goodenough had accumulated fighting the IRS over income he never earned. That number is not large in the abstract. Against years of wage garnishments, bank withdrawals, and the grinding bureaucratic labor of proving you are not someone you have never been, it is what the court put on the damage.

He told his wife the meeting was not in a business office. It wasn't. It was the last sentence of one life and the first of another — and for 32 years, that other life held. Until a nurse in Phoenix reported income he had never earned, and the thread sitting in a DMV file since 1988 finally got pulled. He walked out in 1979 and became Joseph Richard Sandelli, and 32 years later, a DMV file connected Sandelli back to Arthur Gerald Jones.
